items.stem: Which country's constitution (2008) first recognised the rights of nature (Pachamama)?
items.answer: Ecuador
items.markingKey: B. Article 71 of Ecuador's constitution.

items.stem: Outline how granting legal rights to nature could change environmental decision-making.
items.answer: Ecosystems can be represented in court by guardians, so harm to the ecosystem itself becomes legally actionable rather than only harm to human property or health; it shifts law from anthropocentric towards ecocentric values.
items.markingKey: Ecosystems can be represented in court by guardians, so harm to the ecosystem itself becomes legally actionable rather than only harm to human property or health; it shifts law from anthropocentric towards ecocentric values. [1] per valid point, up to [3].

items.stem: Explain why the Montreal Protocol is regarded as a successful environmental agreement.
items.answer: Universal ratification; clear science and identifiable substances; affordable substitutes; a Multilateral Fund to help developing countries; trade restrictions with non-parties; amendments strengthened it over time; ozone layer recovering.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Universal ratification; clear science and identifiable substances; affordable substitutes; a Multilateral Fund to help developing countries; trade restrictions with non-parties; amendments strengthened it over time; ozone layer recovering. (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: State two features that make an international environmental agreement more likely to succeed.
items.answer: Clear targets and timetables; financial and technical support for developing countries; monitoring and reporting; trade or other compliance mechanisms; broad participation.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "environmental law"?
options: A scheme in which beneficiaries pay landowners to manage land to provide ecosystem services such as clean water or carbon storage
The body of national laws, regulations and international agreements that govern human interactions with the environment
The overexploitation of a shared, open-access resource because individuals gain the full benefit of use while the costs are shared by all (Hardin, 1968)
A legally required assessment of the likely environmental effects of a proposed development before a decision is made
items.answer: The body of national laws, regulations and international agreements that govern human interactions with the environment
items.markingKey: B. "environmental law" is the body of national laws, regulations and international agreements that govern human interactions with the environment.

items.stem: "Signing an international agreement immediately makes it binding on a country." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: A state usually must ratify the agreement (often requiring parliamentary approval) and the treaty must enter into force; signature alone signals intent.

items.markingKey: Context (The European Court of Human Rights ruled that Switzerland's inadequate climate policies violated the right to private and family life of older women.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.stem: Explain why environmental problems are often described as market failures.
items.answer: Prices do not include external costs such as pollution or loss of ecosystem services, so goods are overproduced and natural resources overused; many ecosystem services are public goods or open-access, with no market price.

items.stem: Distinguish between use values and non-use values.
items.answer: Use values come from direct or indirect use of a resource (timber, fishing, flood control); non-use values come from knowing it exists or can be passed on (existence and bequest values).

items.stem: The private cost to an airline of producing one passenger flight is $189; the external cost of CO₂ emissions and noise is $87 per passenger flight. Calculate the social cost per unit and state the size of the Pigouvian tax that would internalise the externality.
items.answer: social cost = private + external = 189 + 87 = $276 per unit; Pigouvian tax = $87 per unit (equal to the marginal external cost)
items.markingKey: M1 private + external; A1 $276; A1 tax = $87.

items.stem: Explain the difference between intrinsic value and instrumental value.
items.answer: Intrinsic value is the worth of something in itself regardless of use; instrumental value is worth as a means to human ends, such as timber or recreation.

items.stem: Explain why climate change is considered an issue of environmental justice.
items.answer: High-income countries and wealthy people are responsible for most historical emissions, while low-income countries, small island states and poor communities face the greatest impacts (sea-level rise, drought, floods) with least capacity to adapt.

items.stem: Using New York City's Catskills watershed as an example, explain valuing ecosystem services.
items.answer: In the 1990s the city invested about US$1.5 billion in watershed protection instead of a filtration plant estimated at US$6-8 billion. Protecting natural capital provided clean water more cheaply than built infrastructure.
items.markingKey: Context (In the 1990s the city invested about US$1.5 billion in watershed protection instead of a filtration plant estimated at US$6-8 billion.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Protecting natural capital provided clean water more cheaply than built infrastructure. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to valuing ecosystem services.

items.stem: With reference to Flint water crisis, Michigan (2014-2019), explain how it illustrates distributive and procedural injustice.
items.answer: A switch of water source to save money exposed a majority Black city to lead-contaminated water. Cost-cutting decisions made without community input harmed a low-income population.
items.markingKey: Context (A switch of water source to save money exposed a majority Black city to lead-contaminated water.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Cost-cutting decisions made without community input harmed a low-income population. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to distributive and procedural injustice.

items.stem:
Study the extract from the resource booklet.

Cost-benefit analysis of a coastal mangrove restoration project (present values over 30 years): restoration cost US$12 million; avoided storm damage US$18 million; fisheries benefits US$6 million; carbon storage US$4 million. Using a higher discount rate halves the present value of all benefits.

Discuss what the result shows about the role of value judgements in CBA.
items.answer: The project is worthwhile in both cases, but the benefit is much smaller at a high discount rate; choosing the rate reflects how much we value future generations; non-market values (biodiversity, culture) are not included.
items.markingKey: The project is worthwhile in both cases, but the benefit is much smaller at a high discount rate; choosing the rate reflects how much we value future generations; non-market values (biodiversity, culture) are not included. Award [1] per valid point or correct step, up to [3]; quoted data must include units; points must be drawn from the resource.

items.stem: Briefly analyse two contrasting points of view on the statement: "Granting legal personhood to rivers is an effective way to protect them."
items.answer: Legal personhood can strengthen protection where backed by strong institutions, as in New Zealand, but alone it does not guarantee improvement.
items.markingKey: For: ecosystems gain legal standing. Against: enforcement depends on resources and political will. [4]: [1] for a valid argument for and [1] for its development; [1] for a valid argument against and [1] for its development; generic points with no environmental context are capped at [2].

items.stem: Using the case study and your own knowledge, evaluate the view that carbon taxes are more effective than cap-and-trade schemes in reducing emissions.
items.answer: Both can work; effectiveness depends on the price level, coverage and political design.
items.markingKey: Strengths / supporting points: price certainty; simple to administer; revenue can be recycled (British Columbia, Sweden). Limitations / counter-points: quantity of emissions uncertain; politically unpopular (gilets jaunes); cap-and-trade guarantees an emissions cap. Conclusion: Both can work; effectiveness depends on the price level, coverage and political design. [6]: award [1] for each valid, developed evaluative point (strength or limitation) up to [4], and up to [2] for a balanced, justified conclusion; at least one point must refer explicitly to the case study for full marks.

items.stem: "Environmental justice should be the main consideration in environmental decision-making." Discuss this statement with reference to named examples. [9]
items.answer: Justice is essential to legitimate and lasting decisions, but it should be balanced with ecological integrity and other values.
items.markingKey: Indicative content - arguments supporting the statement: protects vulnerable groups; fair processes increase legitimacy and compliance; human rights obligations. Arguments challenging it: ecocentric values may be overlooked; trade-offs with economic efficiency; difficult to define fairness. items.stem: Discuss, from more than one environmental value system, the view that the economic lens is the most important when making decisions about environmental issues. [9]
items.answer: Economics is influential, but sound decisions require legal compliance and ethical justification, so no single lens should dominate.

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "polluter pays principle".
items.answer: The principle that those who cause pollution should bear the costs of preventing or remedying it
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the principle that those who cause pollution should bear the costs of preventing or remedying it. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: The Dasgupta Review (2021) on the economics of biodiversity was commissioned by:
items.answer: the UK Treasury
items.markingKey: D. It argued that nature should be included in economic decision-making.

items.stem: The UNFCCC principle that recognises different responsibilities of countries is:
items.answer: common but differentiated responsibilities
items.markingKey: common but differentiated responsibilities. Developed countries should take the lead.

items.stem: Distinguish between the economic lens and the ethical lens.
items.answer: The economic lens analyses costs, benefits, incentives and efficiency, often in monetary terms; the ethical lens asks what is right, fair and just, including values that cannot be monetised.
items.markingKey: The economic lens analyses costs, benefits, incentives and efficiency, often in monetary terms; the ethical lens asks what is right, fair and just, including values that cannot be monetised. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why international environmental law is difficult to enforce.
items.answer: States are sovereign and agreements depend on voluntary ratification; there is usually no international police or court with compulsory jurisdiction; states may withdraw (USA from Paris in 2017 and 2025); compliance relies on reporting, peer pressure and trade measures.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: States are sovereign and agreements depend on voluntary ratification; there is usually no international police or court with compulsory jurisdiction; states may withdraw (USA from Paris in 2017 and 2025); compliance relies on reporting, peer pressure and trade measures. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "If something has no market price it has no economic value." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Ecosystem services such as pollination and climate regulation have large economic value even though they are not traded.
items.markingKey: Ecosystem services such as pollination and climate regulation have large economic value even though they are not traded. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between intrinsic value and instrumental value.
items.answer: Intrinsic value is the worth of something in itself regardless of use; instrumental value is worth as a means to human ends, such as timber or recreation.
items.markingKey: Intrinsic value is the worth of something in itself regardless of use; instrumental value is worth as a means to human ends, such as timber or recreation. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Alessia writes: "Cost-benefit analysis gives an objective answer." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: CBA depends on which costs and benefits are included, how they are valued and the discount rate chosen, all of which involve value judgements.
items.markingKey: CBA depends on which costs and benefits are included, how they are valued and the discount rate chosen, all of which involve value judgements. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between international environmental law and national environmental law.
items.answer: National law is passed by a state's legislature and enforced by its courts and agencies; international law is agreed between states through treaties and relies on states to implement it domestically.
items.markingKey: National law is passed by a state's legislature and enforced by its courts and agencies; international law is agreed between states through treaties and relies on states to implement it domestically. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Outline two methods used to value ecosystem services.
items.answer: Market prices (timber, fish); replacement or avoided-cost methods (cost of artificial flood defences avoided by wetlands); travel-cost method (recreation); contingent valuation (willingness to pay surveys).
items.markingKey: Market prices (timber, fish); replacement or avoided-cost methods (cost of artificial flood defences avoided by wetlands); travel-cost method (recreation); contingent valuation (willingness to pay surveys).

items.stem: Distinguish between anthropocentric and biocentric ethics using an example.
items.answer: Anthropocentric: protect a forest because it provides water and timber for people; biocentric: protect it because all living organisms in it have intrinsic value.
items.markingKey: Anthropocentric: protect a forest because it provides water and timber for people; biocentric: protect it because all living organisms in it have intrinsic value.

items.stem: Explain combining legal, economic and ethical lenses, referring in detail to Belo Monte Dam, Brazil and to at least one other example you have studied. [7]
items.answer: The dam on the Xingu River (completed 2019) displaced about 20,000 people and was challenged by Indigenous groups and in court for lack of proper consultation. An economically justified energy project raised legal challenges and ethical concerns about FPIC and justice. A second, contrasting example should be developed in the same way.

items.stem:
Resource booklet summary (Te Awa Tupua (Whanganui River) Act 2017): New Zealand recognised the Whanganui River as a legal person, represented by two guardians, one from the Crown and one from the Whanganui iwi.

Explain what this information reveals about rights of nature in law.
items.answer: Law recognised an Indigenous ecocentric worldview and gave the river standing in its own right.

items.stem: With reference to EU Emissions Trading System, explain in detail the causes and consequences involved in cap-and-trade. [7]
items.answer: Launched in 2005, it covers power, industry and aviation; emissions from covered sectors fell by about 47% from 2005 to 2023. A falling cap and a rising carbon price (over €80 per tonne in 2023) encouraged switching from coal. A second, contrasting example should be developed in the same way.

items.stem:
Resource booklet summary (Tuvalu and sea-level rise): Tuvalu, with a highest point of about 4.6 m, signed the Falepili Union with Australia in 2023 offering migration pathways to its citizens.

Explain what this information reveals about climate justice.
items.answer: A nation with negligible emissions faces loss of territory due to emissions from others.
items.markingKey: A nation with negligible emissions faces loss of territory due to emissions from others. Award [1] for each valid point linking the extract to climate justice, up to [4]; at least one point must use detail from the extract.

items.stem: With reference to Pacific deep-sea mining, explain how it illustrates precaution, economics and ethics.
items.answer: The International Seabed Authority has debated mining regulations, while more than 25 countries had called for a moratorium or precautionary pause by 2024. Demand for battery metals conflicts with precaution, unknown ecosystem value and intergenerational equity.
items.markingKey: Context (The International Seabed Authority has debated mining regulations, while more than 25 countries had called for a moratorium or precautionary pause by 2024.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Demand for battery metals conflicts with precaution, unknown ecosystem value and intergenerational equity. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to precaution, economics and ethics.

items.stem: With reference to the resource booklet and examples you have studied, evaluate the claim: "International environmental agreements are more effective than national laws in tackling environmental problems."
items.answer: International agreements are needed for transboundary issues, but they work only when implemented and enforced through national law.
items.markingKey: Strengths / supporting points: global problems need global cooperation (ozone, climate); set common standards. Limitations / counter-points: enforcement weak; relies on national implementation; withdrawal possible; national laws enforced by courts and agencies. Conclusion: International agreements are needed for transboundary issues, but they work only when implemented and enforced through national law.
